Handle with care: if you would rather follow a fixed menu and station division of labour, rely on colleagues to get through a service peak, or are unwilling to handle purchasing, inventory and expense records, the actual work will not match expectations.

The core output is meals delivered at the agreed time that match the employer's taste and dietary restrictions, with menu, purchasing and expense records kept, not “being able to make a particular dish” or “being able to use a particular machine”.

Low-risk verification: use fictional household members, taste preferences and a dietary restriction list to do one “menu plan—purchasing check—cooking—serving and recording” exercise; it only gauges work preferences and is not equivalent to a qualification, training or hiring.
Central judgement: whether you can, on your own, keep the menu, purchasing, hygiene and records consistent with the employer household's taste, dietary restrictions and daily routine.

Work pace is decided by the employer household's routine, the number of diners, and banquet and holiday arrangements; live-in cooks and per-visit personal cooks differ markedly in time arrangements, pay basis and the tools they provide themselves.

Menu and purchasing, cooking and serving, and kitchen tidying and records are editorial cross-cutting work areas on this page, not three official occupations. Currently 13 tasks 12/1 Core and Supplemental: washing, trimming, cutting and cooking, baking, cooling, packaging, labelling, freezing and reheating instructions, menu planning and purchasing, meals for family and other household staff, menu financial records, kitchen tidying, organising kitchen food events, special diets, family banquets, exploring new dishes and serving are Core; accompanying the employer to a holiday residence is Supplemental. Menu and purchasing

Draw up a menu to the employer's taste and dietary restrictions → plan dishes for family banquets or holiday meals → estimate ingredients and portions from household size and frequency → buy or order ingredients and kitchen supplies → check shelf life and storage conditions by batch → label arrival time and storage location
Menu and purchasing records, confirmation of dietary restrictions and allergen ingredients
Cooking and serving

Wash and cut vegetables, meat and seafood → cook and bake to the employer's recipes and taste → handle special diets and signature dishes → check doneness and seasoning → serve the employer household and their guests and provide refreshments → record output and feedback
Output records and taste feedback, confirmation of stopping on exceptions and reporting
Kitchen tidying and records

Store, tidy and clean the kitchen and cookware → cool, package, label and freeze food as needed → write reheating instructions → record menus, expenses and other administrative matters → check the week's data against physical stock → set out outstanding items and hand over
Where is the boundary between private household cooks and adjacent catering positions?

This table compares private household cooks with adjacent catering positions item by item across seven dimensions: core purpose, main object and basis, core process, main output, responsible party, collaboration and supervision, and boundaries of conclusion; adjacent positions all work in food preparation settings, but whether the people served are a single household or the public, who decides the menu, whether purchasing and expense records are kept, and the food-safety chain of responsibility do not transfer simply because positions are adjacent; comparisons must check the actual duties item by item.
Core purpose
In a private household, plan menus, purchase, cook and serve to one family's taste and dietary and nutritional restrictions, and keep menu, purchasing and expense records.

Core purposes of adjacent positions: head cooks and chefs are responsible for menu design and output standards; food service managers are responsible for outlet or catering operations, costs and staff; restaurant cooks serve continuously in the back of house to customer orders; institution and cafeteria cooks serve a fixed population in bulk to a cyclical menu; fast food cooks prepare to order in a limited-menu restaurant; food preparation workers are responsible for upstream preparation such as washing and cutting.
Main object and basis

The employer household's taste preferences, dietary and nutritional restrictions, number of diners and routine, banquet and holiday arrangements, ingredient batches and the expense ledger; the basis is the employer's requirements, ingredient labels and applicable food hygiene requirements.

Objects and bases of adjacent positions: menus and cost sheets (chefs and managers), full recipes and orders (restaurant cooks), cyclical menus and dietary restrictions (institution and cafeteria cooks), fast food recipes and order tickets (fast food cooks), prep lists (preparation workers).
Core process

Draw up the menu and estimate portions → purchase and check by batch → wash, cut, cook and bake → season and plate and serve → tidy the kitchen and store and freeze → record menus, expenses and handover.

Processes of adjacent positions: menu and cost accounting, scheduling and purchasing, continuous heating and plating to order, bulk cooking and portioning to a cyclical menu, bulk heating and boxing to order, washing, cutting and preparing.
Main output
Meals delivered at agreed times that match the employer's taste and dietary restrictions, together with verifiable menu, purchasing and expense records.

Outputs of adjacent positions: a costable menu and gross margin, operating reports, per-customer dishes, bulk meals and temperature-control records, fast food finished products, prepared semi-finished ingredients.
Responsible party

The private household cook is responsible for menu planning, purchasing checks, cooking and serving, applying dietary restrictions, tidying the kitchen and the accuracy of records; the household employment arrangement, purchasing budget and expense approval are decided by the employer.

Responsible parties of adjacent positions: chefs and managers are responsible for menus, costs and people management; restaurant and fast food cooks are responsible for single-customer or single-order output; institution and cafeteria cooks are responsible for bulk meal portions, temperature control and records; preparation workers are responsible for prep specifications.
Collaboration and supervision

In practice the cook may work independently or organise food events and collaborate, and no share of positions working alone was obtained. Accompanying the employer on holiday is Supplemental, and specific communication and arrangements are checked against the service agreement; exceptions are held back, and the employer's agreement cannot prove safety or substitute for the applicable basis for handling.

Collaboration of adjacent positions: chefs and managers assign tasks and schedules; restaurant cooks align timing with the plating and food-running roles; institution and cafeteria cooks collaborate by station and meal service period; fast food cooks check orders with the counter; preparation workers receive prep specification requirements.
Boundaries of conclusion

Similar position names do not mean interchangeable roles: whether the public is served, who decides the menu, and whether purchasing and expense records are kept determine the scope of authorisation and where responsibility lies.

The preparation levels and qualification requirements of adjacent positions do not apply to this occupation and must be checked item by item against each occupation's official material and the employer's rules.
Key occupational judgements

Six recurring professional judgements: whether the employer's taste and dietary restrictions are checked; whether ingredients and portions match the number of diners; whether raw-cooked zoning and allergen isolation are in place; whether heating and storage temperatures meet the standard; whether purchasing, inventory and expenses are recorded as agreed; and whether ingredient exceptions and household feedback are handled according to procedure and handed over.

Before cooking, check taste preferences, food avoidances, allergens and dietary restrictions item by item (low salt, low sugar, vegetarian, soft food and so on) and confirm the number of diners; treating restrictions as a verbal impression rather than applying them to a specific meal will pass the risk on to members of the employer household and their guests.

Editorial suggestion: estimate ingredients from the menu and the number of diners and recheck portions, and check batch and shelf life when purchasing; whether estimation causes shortages or waste must be checked against actual usage, keeping assumptions and physical check records, and experience-based estimation alone does not invalidate recording.

Raw and cooked ingredients, knives and chopping boards must be handled separately and cleaned and disinfected, and allergen-containing ingredients stored and labelled separately; in a home kitchen with shared stations confusion is more likely, so separate checking is essential.

Check cooking, storage and reheating temperature and time against the applicable dish and equipment requirements and keep records; confirm with a food thermometer, as appearance and tasting cannot prove that suspect food is safe. This round obtained no ranking of common hazards or complete handling conditions for every food.
Judgement four: do heating and storage temperatures meet the standard?

Editorial suggestion: record the menu, purchasing, inventory, expenses, batches and storage locations as agreed with the employer; unclear records may impede expense checks and rotation, and the actual effect and other material must be checked, without assuming simultaneous loss of control.
Judgement five: are purchasing, inventory and expenses recorded as agreed?

For spoilage, foreign objects and allergy risk, first hold back the affected food, check batch and temperature and discuss alternatives; resuming requires an applicable safety basis, and the employer's agreement alone cannot release it. Handover keeps outstanding items in the actual form used, without uniformly treating oral handover as invalid.

Core: trimming, cutting and cooking vegetables and meat, baking and exploring new dishes; the literal “wash” task does not mean all raw meat must be rinsed. U.S. FoodSafety.gov household guidance lists clean, separate, confirm cooking with a thermometer, and chill promptly, and states explicitly not to wash raw meat, poultry, eggs and seafood so as to avoid spreading contamination. It is U.S. household food-safety guidance, not Chinese law; this page has no complete temperature handling procedure for every dish, and exceptions are held back until an applicable basis is obtained, since the employer's agreement cannot prove food safety.

Core: cooking and serving meals for the family and household staff, family banquets and special diets; Supplemental: catering while accompanying the employer on holiday. The specific scope follows the task authorisation, and accompanying the employer is not uniformly Core.

Tidying, storage and reheating ｜ tidy the kitchen and keep instructions ｜ store, tidy and clean the kitchen and cookware, cool, package, label and freeze food as needed, write reheating methods, and maintain raw-cooked zoning and cleaning and disinfection.

Records and handover ｜ record menus, expenses and matters ｜ record administrative matters such as menus, purchasing, inventory and expenses, explain shortages and losses to the employer, and set out unresolved exceptions and items to be confirmed and hand them over.
Work context and working conditions

Private household kitchen work may involve standing, hand use, menu purchasing and communication requirements; the specific space, collaboration and rotation are checked against the actual residence and service agreement, and working alone is not guaranteed for most positions.

Current 57 work context questions: 54% daily in a climate-controlled indoor environment and 27% weekly rather than daily; outdoors in all weather 42% never and 50% yearly rather than monthly, and non-climate-controlled indoors 50% never, 19% weekly and 31% yearly. The last two questions do not show complete daily responses and cannot be filled in with 0, and the actual residence's ventilation and space must be checked.

Main materials and equipment ｜ ingredients and seasonings, the home kitchen's stove, oven, steaming gear and refrigeration and freezer equipment, knives and chopping boards, tableware and washing equipment, a food thermometer, preservation and labelling supplies, and menu and purchasing record tools; the equipment list comes from this occupation's tasks and work activities and is not a purchasing recommendation; a per-visit personal cook may also provide their own knives and some tools.

Then wash, cut, cook and bake in menu order and check doneness, and serve at the agreed time; when ingredient exceptions, allergy risk or equipment faults occur, stop using them and agree an alternative with the employer; after the meal, tidy the kitchen, store or freeze food and record the menu and expenses.

Work week: 27% over 40 / 35% about 40 / 38% under 40 hours; 50% irregular and 46% regular, which are U.S. respondent answers, not Chinese rotation rules.

Currently contact with others 21%/42%, continually and most of the time, and face-to-face 29% daily; teamwork 15%/15%/46%, extremely important, very important and not important, and coordinating 15% very important and 42% not important, with some responses not shown. This does not establish that most work alone or allow direct comparison of the collaboration scale of two occupations; the actual kitchen organisation is checked separately.

Currently responsibility for health and safety 27%/27%, very high and high; 35% make daily decisions. Consequences of error show 12%/15%/38%/27%, extremely serious, very serious, fairly serious and not serious, with other responses not shown and no old total filled in. This is not an accident rate, a legal allocation of responsibility or working hours; records follow the service agreement and applicable requirements.

Currently 44% have daily routine protection, accuracy 19%/42%/23%, extremely important, very important and important, and 50% never sit; 23% face daily burn, cut and sting exposure and 12% daily noise. The U.S. respondent answers to several questions are not an actual injury rate or Chinese conditions, and the supply categories do not require a full set for every person; actual selection is based on station assessment.

Restaurant cooks (O*NET-SOC 35-2014.00, adjacent segment)

Serve continuously in a restaurant back-of-house according to customer orders and the menu: the dish range is wider and there are more stations, requiring both reproducing flavours to recipe and aligning timing with the plating and food-running roles at peak times.

The key difference from private household cooks is serving public customers, with the restaurant deciding the menu and the service pace; employment was 1,460,200 in 2024, and the O*NET growth category is “much faster than average (7% or higher)”.
Better suited to people willing to collaborate on service in a faster-paced, multi-dish environment and able to accept evening and weekend shifts.
Institution and cafeteria cooks (O*NET-SOC 35-2012.00, adjacent segment)
Cook and portion in bulk to a cyclical menu for fixed populations such as schools, hospitals and enterprise and institutional canteens, and often keep usage and expenditure records.

The key difference is serving a fixed population to a cyclical menu, mainly in bulk, with the people served not being a single household; employment was 466,100 in 2024, and the O*NET growth category is “slower than average (1% to 2%)”.
Better suited to people willing to produce consistently to a fixed menu and fixed periods and able to accept long periods of standing and collective collaboration.
Fast food cooks (O*NET-SOC 35-2011.00, adjacent segment)
The key difference is cooking to customer order, with a fixed menu and random portion counts; employment was 669,500 in 2024, and the O*NET growth category is “decline (-14%)”.
Better suited to people who can accept a high degree of repetition, work to a standard and want to start work relatively quickly.
Food preparation workers (O*NET-SOC 35-2021.00, adjacent occupation)

The key difference is that there is no responsibility for menu planning and expense records; employment was 902,700 in 2024, the O*NET growth category is “decline (-1% or lower)”, and it often serves as the entry point into the catering system.
Better suited to people who want to start from preparation and gradually learn menus and cooking.
Chefs and head cooks (O*NET-SOC 35-1011.00, adjacent occupation)

The key difference from this occupation is management responsibility and menu leadership: taking on menu design and cost accounting, staff scheduling and training, and setting output standards; the preparation level is Job Zone 3, and employment was 197,300 in 2024.
Better suited to people who have built up output experience, are willing to take on staff and cost management responsibility, and want to lead the menu direction.
Food service managers (O*NET-SOC 11-9051.00, adjacent occupation)

The key difference from this occupation is operational and people management responsibility: a median annual wage of 69,390 dollars (2025), employment of 352,800 in 2024, and the O*NET growth category “much faster than average (5% to 6%)”.
Better suited to people interested in operations, budgeting and people management and willing to take on compliance and scheduling responsibility.

values: Fictional work-order material (practice input)

Fictional scenario: a fictional family banquet on Friday evening has 8 people, of whom 1 household member is allergic to nuts, 1 needs low-salt soft food and 1 does not eat animal offal; in this week's purchasing records a batch of chilled poultry is marked with an arrival date of Tuesday and a shelf life to the following Monday, but the fridge temperature log shows two occasions this week above 4 degrees Celsius with only “adjusted” written.

Material provided: this week's menu and taste preference list; a note of household members' allergies and dietary restrictions; the number of diners and the time arrangement; the purchasing batch and shelf-life ledger; the fridge and finished-product temperature records; the note on kitchen utensil and chopping board zoning.

Material not provided: the specific duration and cause of the higher temperature, whether the affected poultry has already been used in earlier meals, the confirmation process for deciding whether to discard it, and the employer's preference for a substitute menu. If these conditions are needed in the exercise, state your assumptions and whom you would need to confirm them with.
Task requirements

Write a one-page weekly handling and banquet plan covering menu and dietary restriction checks, the judgement and handling of the affected ingredients, purchasing top-ups and inventory rotation, cooking and finished-product temperature requirements, serving times and portion arrangements, the situations that require stopping use or confirming with the employer, and the matters to be recorded and handed over.
The plan must state which data come from the exercise material and which are still assumptions, and must say whether it relies on the menu, the temperature records or the utensil zoning note.
Reference deliverable (derivable from the exercise material)

The plan should include: checks (apply the 3 restrictions to specific meals and utensils separately, and match the 8 portions to dishes one by one); ingredient judgement (the chilled poultry from the temperature anomaly period must be held back and confirmed with the employer, and must not be released on the strength of an “adjusted” record alone); purchasing top-ups (determine the top-up list from the banquet headcount and existing stock, and keep receipts and batches); cooking and temperature (check finished-product core temperature and cooling and freezing times, with separate utensils and stations for allergen meals); serving and records (serve according to the time arrangement, set out the menu, purchasing, expenses and losses, and register the items still to be confirmed).
The reference deliverable lists only the elements that should be included and does not require wording identical to the example; explaining the basis for your judgement is enough.

This exercise tests only taste and dietary restriction checking, purchasing and temperature awareness, and the ability to organise records; it does not evaluate any real household's meal safety and does not constitute an employment or qualification judgement or advice on real food-safety or dietary handling.

entries.answer: Plan menus to the employer's taste and dietary or nutritional restrictions, buy or order ingredients and kitchen supplies, wash and cut vegetables and meat and bake bread and pastries, cook and serve in a private household, prepare for family banquets and holiday meals, store, tidy and clean the kitchen and cookware, cool, package, label and freeze food and provide reheating instructions, record administrative matters such as menus and expenses, and cook at a holiday residence with the employer as needed.
entries.question: What does the daily work of private household cooks involve?

entries.answer: Private household cooks serve one family, with the menu set by the employer's taste and dietary restrictions, and they often keep purchasing and expense records; restaurant cooks serve public customers with a wider dish range and cook to order; institution and cafeteria cooks serve a fixed population in bulk to a cyclical menu.
entries.question: How do private household cooks differ from restaurant cooks and institution and cafeteria cooks?

entries.answer: Menu and recipe organisation, purchasing lists and inventory alerts, expense records and scheduling can be assisted by systems, and programmed equipment and temperature logging can also reduce manual steps; but applying taste and dietary restrictions, purchasing checks, heat and seasoning judgement, allergen isolation, ingredient exception handling and household communication still depend on on-site staff. Technology exposure does not equal organisational adoption or the disappearance of jobs.
entries.question: How will AI affect or replace private household cooks?

entries.answer: What can be checked is change at the task level: three task groups — menu, purchasing and expense information, cooking and service pace, and temperature, storage and records — can be partly taken over by tools; this page has no occupation-specific adoption rate or displacement data.
entries.question: For which tasks of private household cooks is there evidence of AI-driven change?

entries.answer: Menu planning and taste checking, purchasing and batch checks, heat control and seasoning, handling dietary restrictions and allergens, storage and reheating instructions, and the checking ability needed when using menu, purchasing and bookkeeping tools.
entries.question: Faced with AI, which abilities should private household cooks still focus on verifying?

entries.answer: In the United States the 2025 median hourly wage is 23.05 dollars and the median annual wage is 47,940 dollars (the single-occupation measure for 35-2013.00), with percentiles of 36,090/40,630/47,940/55,450/91,130 dollars a year; that measure excludes self-employed personal cooks. No occupation-level wage figures were obtained for mainland China, and this page treats this as a gap rather than filling it in with industry averages.
entries.question: How much do private household cooks generally earn, and how should this be compared?

entries.answer: The U.S. preparation level is Job Zone 3, and respondent education requirements show 38% stating a postsecondary certificate is needed, 31% a high school diploma or equivalent and 15% below high school, with skills coming mainly from related work experience and on-the-job training; the common starting point for household meal service in mainland China is junior or senior high school, and some require health management and hygiene training.
entries.question: What education do private household cooks need, and how should they train?

entries.answer: There is no uniform mandatory licence in the United States; in mainland China health management and hygiene training are common prerequisites, and the Chinese cuisine chef vocational skill grade is usually not a threshold for household meal service, with specific requirements following the employment agreement and the competent authority's rules.
entries.question: Do you have to obtain a certificate to work as a private household cook?

entries.answer: First complete one “menu plan—purchasing check—cooking—serving and recording” exercise using the fictional material on this page, or do one household meal shadowing experience, and then check the target household's taste requirements, dining frequency and employment agreement.

entries.answer: U.S. official projections show the growth rate for this occupation over 2024—2034 as “much faster than average (5% to 6%)”, with about 5,300 job openings over the projection period; but the occupation is small and household employment mostly depends on direct agreement, and hours and income change with the employer household, so it must be checked against local actual demand.

The 90th percentile is a wage position within the OEWS covered population, not a senior grade; the original table does not break down the causes by number of households, live-in status, duties or region, so it does not extrapolate an individual quote.

BLS table 1.2 private household cooks 35-2013: employment rising from 35,400 in 2025 to a projected 37,200 in 2035, a published net increase of 1,800 and growth of 5.1%, with an average of 5,000 openings per year (including growth and replacement), and the self-employed accounting for 79.7%. OOH/O*NET round the growth rate to 5%. The employment projection includes the self-employed while the wage coverage differs; openings are not a ten-year total, net increases, current hiring or a hiring probability. The OEWS method explicitly excludes the self-employed, people directly employed by private households and unpaid family members. O*NET currently still publishes 2025 wages for 35-2013, which can be read only as wages for the jobs covered by that survey and do not represent all private household direct employment, self-employed per-visit quotes, profit or all employment income; per-visit service does not automatically equal self-employment, and the actual employment status must be checked.
The growth rate is a relative change over the projection period; the net change in headcount over the same period and job openings are different measures and cannot substitute for one another.
Average annual openings include growth and replacement and are not a ten-year total, net additions, current hiring or a hiring rate.

description.text: Private household cooks (O*NET-SOC 35-2013.00) plan menus, purchase, cook and serve in private homes to the employer's taste and dietary restrictions: this covers menus and purchasing, dietary and nutritional restrictions, family banquets and holiday meals, kitchen tidying and inventory, freezing and storage and reheating instructions, and menu and expense records; it includes the U.S. 2025 median hourly wage of 23.05 dollars, a 2024—2034 growth rate of “much faster than average (5% to 6%)” and about 5,300 job openings over the projection period, the mainland China occupation-level wage gap and industry proxy boundary, burn and scald and food-safety risk control, and the boundaries of the fictional exercises.

subject.name: Private household cooks
subject.summary: Private household cooks (Cooks, Private Household) correspond in the United States to O*NET-SOC 35-2013.00: in a private home, planning menus, purchasing ingredients, cooking and serving to the employer's taste and dietary and nutritional restrictions, possibly also handling family banquets and holiday meals, tidying the kitchen and tableware, inventory and purchasing, freezing and storage and reheating instructions, and menu and expense records; this covers both live-in cooks employed by a single family and per-visit personal cooks (the latter often self-employed or contracted, under a different statistical measure); there is no corresponding occupational subclass on the Chinese side, and it must be checked separately against domestic service and skill grade entities.
